A GP assigns jointly Gaussian values to every finite set of input locations with mean $m$ and covariance kernel $k$. With Gaussian observation noise $\sigma^2$, let $K_y=K(X,X)+\sigma^2I$. The posterior mean at $x_*$ is $m_*+k_*^TK_y^{-1}(y-m)$ and variance is $k_{**}-k_*^TK_y^{-1}k_*$. [1](https://gaussianprocess.org/gpml/)

Use Cholesky solves, not an explicit inverse; dense factorization costs $O(N^3)$ time and $O(N^2)$ storage. For maximization, expected improvement is $(\mu-f_{best}-\xi)\Phi(z)+\sigma\phi(z)$ with $z=(\mu-f_{best}-\xi)/\sigma$, using the zero-variance limit when needed. GPs are a strong Bayesian-optimization baseline for expensive, modest-dimensional smooth problems, not universally the gold standard. Kernel mismatch, noise, constraints, and large/high-dimensional datasets motivate alternative surrogates or approximations.
